artworks.title: Allegorical Portrait of Urania, Muse of Astronomy
artworks.description: In this elegant Rococo allegory, the French portraitist Louis Tocqué casts his sitter in the guise of Urania, the Muse who presided over astronomy and the order of the heavens. She rests one hand upon a celestial globe — her unmistakable attribute, its surface marked with the constellations — while the other holds a slender pointer for tracing the stars, the small compass-like instrument by which she measures the sky. The conceit of the 'portrait historié,' dressing a noblewoman as the heavenly Muse, flatters her learning by aligning her with the daughter of Zeus and Mnemosyne who, in Hesiod's Theogony, sings of the wheeling cosmos.

artworks.title: Urania, Muse of Astronomy
artworks.description: The Roman Baroque painter Giovanni Baglione depicts Urania, the celestial Muse, seated with a great star-strewn globe of the heavens at her side, the constellations charted across its sphere. As one of the nine Muses born to Zeus and the memory-goddess Mnemosyne, Urania alone governed astronomy, and ancient authors made her the Muse who taught mortals to read the courses of the stars. Baglione gives her the contemplative gravity of a heavenly philosopher, her gaze turned upward toward the sky whose motions she interprets — the lone star among her sister Muses who answers to the cosmos itself.

artworks.title: Urania, Muse of Astronomy
artworks.description: Attributed to the late-Baroque Roman painter Francesco Trevisani, this canvas isolates Urania among the nine Muses as the patroness of the stars. She is shown with the celestial globe and pointer that ancient iconography assigned to her alone, the instruments with which she charts the firmament. Daughter of Zeus and Mnemosyne and named for the 'heavenly' realm (Ourania, 'the celestial one'), she embodies the Greek conviction that the study of the night sky was itself a form of divine inspiration, the Muse turning the order of the heavens into knowledge and song.
